Give reasons, why you like him/her/it. 100 Films and Theatre A Reading Rendezvous with Ray It was a unique friendship that developed between a French-Canadian priest and one of the world’s greatest film directors, and had a singular impact on Bengali films both A academically and practically. It was enroute to India in1961, N at a stopover in New York, that 26-year- old Fr. Gaston Roberge was acquainted with the works of Satyajit Ray A through the Apu Trilogy. He found the world of Apu so G fascinating that he saw all three films in one sitting; and there began his longstanding love affair with the people of India N and Bengali cinema and culture, which led to path-breaking Gaston Roberge A work in those fields. In his latest book, Satyajit Ray, Essays:1970-2005, a compilation of his essays as the name suggests, being published by L Manohar Publishers, New Delhi, Roberge provides a scholarly, original analysis of Ray’s E works, giving an insight into the greatness of Ray both as a person and as an artist. T “The Apu Trilogy was, in fact, my first portal to West Bengal and its people,” he told Frontline. In his youth , all he k,new of Bengal was through Mircea Eliade’s La Nuit Bengalie, T some of Tagore’s poems, and a Reader’s Digest article on Mother Teresa. If the harsh image of poverty brRought out by the article on the “Saint of the Slums” haunted him, Apu’s world came as a reassurance. “No. Apu, Sarbajaya, even Harihar did not need my help-but E how not to love them? I thought it was fortunate C that I would soon be among them,” he wrote. S Roberge does not endorse the accusation of Ray’s detractors that the master director made his reputation selling India’s poverty to the West. “What struck me most was not the material poverty depicted in the films, but the enormous spiritual poverty of some rich people is much more deplorable than material poverty,” he said. Roberge does not speak with the arrogance of the West. “I was here on a quest to know the world and in the process know myself. I did not come here to 101 A N A G N A L E T convert. In fact, I am the one who got converted,” he said. , But it took him nine years after reaching Calcutta (now Kolkata) and joining St. T Xavier’s College, to muster up the confidence to meet Ray in person. “Although I wanted to R meet him right away, I didn’t want to just go and see him like he was a living museum piece. I wanted to prepare myself, get to know his works more, so that when we met, there could be E a worthwhile dialogue,” he said. When they finally met, it was the beginning of a close C friendship that lasted 22 years- until Ray’s death in 1992. S “It was a very quiet friendship that developed over the years. Manikda [as Ray was affectionately called by his friends] was a shy person and always very discreet about displaying his emotions,” said Roberge. Though to outsiders, Ray’s massive stature- physical and intellectual- might have made him come across as cold, aloof and even intimidating, he was in reality a very simple and unassuming man with a subtle sense of humour. It was an unspoken arrangement between the two of them to meet on Sundays at 9 a.m. at Ray’s residence on Bishop Lefroy Road, Kolkata. Ray would invite Roberge over for private screenings of his latest films and welcomed comments on them. But this happened only after the friendship had cemented, for in the early days of their dialogue Ray’s shyness prevented him from talking about his own films. 102 Films and Theatre “He was even shy of receiving compliments,” said Roberge. To Roberge, the greatest mark of Ray’s appreciation for him was that he often addressed the French-speaking priest in Bengali, “in spite of my lack of elegance in that language, and the fact that Ray knew both English and Bengali so well.” “Ray’s screenplay manuscripts were an art by themselves,” Roberge says, “hand- written in Bengali, with notes in English for his set-designer, with sketches here and there, and occasional staff notation of fragments of music”. One Sunday morning, Roberge found A Ray in a disturbed mood. A few well –known personalities of the city had visited him earlier N to go through some of his manuscripts. After they left Ray found the Charulatha screenplay missing. Ray was almost sure who the culprit was. “I asked him whether he was planning to A take any action, and he said no, and explained to me that he did not want to hurt the reputation G of the person. I was absolutely stunned by his humane concern,” said Roberge. N Like Rabindranath Tagore, Ray strode his time like a colossus. Roberge writes, “It is as if all Bengal was in Manikda: the rich and the poor, the powerful and the humble, the A peasants and the city persons, children, teenagers, adults and old people, men and women.” L Philosophically too, Roberge feels, Ray took off where Tagore signed out. If one E compares the last major prose piece by Tagore, “ Shabhyatar Sankat” ( Crisis of Civilisation), T which he wrote at the beginning of the Second World War, which contains his immortal , T R E C S 103 dictum that in spite of what was happening it would be a sin to lose faith in Man, and the last three films of Ray- Ganashatru, Shakha Prashakha, and Agantuk- the analogy becomes clear. “In these thrAee films Ray was at his most personal and when some an image from N critics saw the films as didactic and Pater Panchali verbose,A he felt deeply hurt. For, in these last films, Satyajit was G directly talking to us, conveying his personal message on society and civilization. If the impulse that motivated his earlier films N was aesthetics, in the last three it was self-expression. And there we were denying him his A right to speak. As the saying goes, no one is a prophet in one’s own country,” said Roberge. An agnostic throughout his life, it is possibLle, Roberge feels, that in the face of death Ray was searching for an answer. This was suggested by some of the music that he used in Shakha E Prashakha. T The last time the two fr iends met, Ray was in hospital, on his deathbed. It was a , Sunday and Roberge, true to habit, arrived on the dot at 9 a.m. “He had grown so weak that he T looked frail as a child. I did not stay long, and as I was leaving, Manikda said, ‘Bhalo laglo’ R [it was nice]. Those were his last words to me,” said Roberge. E One important fallout of this friendship was the establishment of Chitrabani, a C communication and film institute, the first of its kind in West Bengal, which Roberge founded in 1970 and to which Ray, as a token of friendship, lent his name as co-founder. Ray was in S the first governing body and after a few terms readily agreed to be the institute’s adviser. Roberge arranged most of the initial funding from Canadian agencies. “I had no reservations applying for them, for I feel richer countries in the West are indebted to countries like India,” he said. For 26 years Roberge was the director of Chitrabani and under him the institute not only produced important documentary features, but also became breeding ground for local talent for film-making… Frontline, July29-August 11, 2006 104 Films and Theatre Glossary en route (adv) : on the way stopover (n) : a halt in a long journey path-breaking (adj) : totally new A portal (n) : an entrance N trilogy (n) : a set of three films with the same artists or A characters G haunted (v) : obsessed N accusation (n) : the act of charging somebody A detractors (n) : people who criticise L arrogance (n) : shEowing pride muster up confidence (idiomT) : gain confidence dictum (n) ,: a statement that is believed to be true and followed T analogy (n) : a feature that is similar R aesthetics (n) : the art of judging beauty E falloCut (n) : result Sagnostic (n) : a person who does not know whether God exists Comprehension I. It was enroute to India in1961, N at a stopover in New York, that 26-year- old Fr. Gaston Roberge was acquainted with the works of Satyajit Ray A through the Apu Trilogy. He found the world of Apu so G fascinating that he saw all three films in one sitting; and there began his longstanding love affair with the people of India N and Bengali cinema and culture, which led to path-breaking Gaston Roberge A work in those fields. In his latest book, Satyajit Ray, Essays:1970-2005, a compilation of his essays as the name suggests, being published by L Manohar Publishers, New Delhi, Roberge provides a scholarly, original analysis of Ray’s E works, giving an insight into the greatness of Ray both as a person and as an artist. T “The Apu Trilogy was, in fact, my first portal to West Bengal and its people,” he told Frontline. In his youth , all he k,new of Bengal was through Mircea Eliade’s La Nuit Bengalie, T some of Tagore’s poems, and a Reader’s Digest article on Mother Teresa. If the harsh image of poverty brRought out by the article on the “Saint of the Slums” haunted him, Apu’s world came as a reassurance. “No. Apu, Sarbajaya, even Harihar did not need my help-but E how not to love them? I thought it was fortunate C that I would soon be among them,” he wrote. S Roberge does not endorse the accusation of Ray’s detractors that the master director made his reputation selling India’s poverty to the West. “What struck me most was not the material poverty depicted in the films, but the enormous spiritual poverty of some rich people is much more deplorable than material poverty,” he said. Roberge does not speak with the arrogance of the West. “I was here on a quest to know the world and in the process know myself. I did not come here to 101 A N A G N A L E T convert. In fact, I am the one who got converted,” he said. , But it took him nine years after reaching Calcutta (now Kolkata) and joining St. T Xavier’s College, to muster up the confidence to meet Ray in person. “Although I wanted to R meet him right away, I didn’t want to just go and see him like he was a living museum piece. I wanted to prepare myself, get to know his works more, so that when we met, there could be E a worthwhile dialogue,” he said. When they finally met, it was the beginning of a close C friendship that lasted 22 years- until Ray’s death in 1992. S “It was a very quiet friendship that developed over the years. Manikda [as Ray was affectionately called by his friends] was a shy person and always very discreet about displaying his emotions,” said Roberge. Though to outsiders, Ray’s massive stature- physical and intellectual- might have made him come across as cold, aloof and even intimidating, he was in reality a very simple and unassuming man with a subtle sense of humour. It was an unspoken arrangement between the two of them to meet on Sundays at 9 a.m. at Ray’s residence on Bishop Lefroy Road, Kolkata. Ray would invite Roberge over for private screenings of his latest films and welcomed comments on them. But this happened only after the friendship had cemented, for in the early days of their dialogue Ray’s shyness prevented him from talking about his own films. 102 Films and Theatre “He was even shy of receiving compliments,” said Roberge. To Roberge, the greatest mark of Ray’s appreciation for him was that he often addressed the French-speaking priest in Bengali, “in spite of my lack of elegance in that language, and the fact that Ray knew both English and Bengali so well.” “Ray’s screenplay manuscripts were an art by themselves,” Roberge says, “hand- written in Bengali, with notes in English for his set-designer, with sketches here and there, and occasional staff notation of fragments of music”. One Sunday morning, Roberge found A Ray in a disturbed mood. A few well –known personalities of the city had visited him earlier N to go through some of his manuscripts. After they left Ray found the Charulatha screenplay missing. Ray was almost sure who the culprit was. “I asked him whether he was planning to A take any action, and he said no, and explained to me that he did not want to hurt the reputation G of the person. I was absolutely stunned by his humane concern,” said Roberge. N Like Rabindranath Tagore, Ray strode his time like a colossus. Roberge writes, “It is as if all Bengal was in Manikda: the rich and the poor, the powerful and the humble, the A peasants and the city persons, children, teenagers, adults and old people, men and women.” L Philosophically too, Roberge feels, Ray took off where Tagore signed out. If one E compares the last major prose piece by Tagore, “ Shabhyatar Sankat” ( Crisis of Civilisation), T which he wrote at the beginning of the Second World War, which contains his immortal , T R E C S 103

L As for songs, Aha naa pelli anta still reverberates in marriages and Vivaaha E bhojanambu is yet another must. T An entire repertoire was added to the Telugu dictionary by the film. Take for example Talpam used for denoting a cot or a bed. Were Telugus using Gilpam as an antonym of it till , the movie's advent? NorT did anyone tell so emphatically until Ghatothkacha that Evaru puttinchakunte maatalela pudathayi and hence if friends are to be called Asamadiyulu R then enemies could be termed E Tasamadiyulu. Will anyone forget the expression veyandira veediko C veeratadu? No exception to hai hai S sodara and hai hai naayaka . The story itself is woven around the love of Sasirekha- Abhimanyu. With Krishna and Balarama having difference of opinion over it, their wives too take sides as is inevitable in any family. To introduce the theme , the director uses a magic box, (an equivalent of a TV 116 Films and Theatre screen) which displays whatever is dear to the viewer's heart. Sasirekha naturally sees Abhimanyu and Balarama gets to see his sishya, Duryodhana on it. His wife laps up the sight of an array of jewellery and the audience laughed heartily because A they knew that someone back home was equally attached Nto the riches. When Balarama curtly tells his A sister, " Subhadra! Aagadalu, G aghaayityalu naaku paniki raavu", when he was confronted with the latter's N indignation at his decision to separate Sasirekha and Abhimanyu , womenfolk amonAg the viewers sighed recalling their own tribulations in the hands of such brothers. L Frame after frame impacts vieEwers with similarities. The greatness of the director lies here- he successfully reduces all characters to ordinary mortals displaying all the follies T of human beings except Ghatothkacha and Krishna. And then he injects into the Yadava household a Telugu atmosphere , full with its simile, imagery, adage, sarcasm and wit. , T The result — a feast for the eyes and soul. That is Maya Bazaar for you. Mind you, this is a story of PRaandavas and Kauravas with the Yadavas pitching in. But one never sees the Paandavas throughout the film. We E only hear of them. C If any NRI asks you to suggest ways to teach Telugu culture just ask him or her to S introduce them to Maya Bazaar first. Further, if they seek to know about their uncles, aunts and cousins back home, bring in their names , “look, this is your Balarama…” Any better way of doing it? Then onwards it's all Laahiri, laahiri, laahiri lo… -The Hindu, 21 April 2006 117 Glossary VFX : Visual Effects shortened to Visual FX and then to VFX the vicinity (n) : the area around a particular place reverberate (v) : have a strong effect on people for a long time repertoire (n) : all that a performer can do advent (n) : arrival A array (n) : an impressive collection of things indignation (n) : a feeling of anger N sarcasm (n) : a way of using words that are the opposite of what one A means to make fun of somebody G Comprehension N I. They call me ‘a bird in a cage’. (Goes out G disgusted taking his school bag.) ***** N Mother : Money, money, money. He alwayAs needs money. This is not a kid. It's an apparition. L Father : (coming) Why are you shouting, Sarala? What did you say? E Mother : Didn't you hear? An apparition. T Father : Who is the apparition? , Mother : Who else couTld I mean? It's your son. Father : Not youRr son? He needs money? Mother : YesE, he needs money. He watches movies. His life is movies. He doesn't care to study. All the children in the street are doing very well. But this devil ...... (Starts C banging her head against the wall. No wounds.No blood) S Father : No, Sarala. No, don't do it. (Mother falls down and father brings a glass of water.) Father : Sarala..., Sarala...., have some water. (A pause) Father : Sarala, we have to understand certain things. Mother : (Having drunk water) As if you have understood.... . You don't worry about anything. He doesn't study at all. He is after movies. 124 Films and Theatre

Father : Wait! I'll find out. ***** Father : Suhas, you didn't take your bicycle today. You didn't take your lunch box. You look tired...... . Suhas : Amma doesn't understand me. She always makes fuss of me. She always wants me to do one thing; study.... study..... study. I want to go to a film. That too once A a week. All my friends are going. I too want to go. Is it wrong on my part? N Father : Why don't you try to understand your mother's concern? She is worried a lot about your future. A Suhas : But I am all right in my studies. I think, watchinGg a film once a week, that too, watching a good film is not a sin. N Father : Which film did you want to watch? A Suhas : "Life of Pi". It's an interesting movie with high technical values. L Father : All right, my boy. E ***** T Father : Sarala, the boy didn't want to do anything bad. , Mother : But I have my own fears. T Father : I do understand. Your fears may have reasons. But what Suhas wanted was just R 100 rupees. And that too for watching an interesting film. E Mother : Maybe I was wrong. We'll ask Suhas to go to the film. He is such a nice boy. He C never troubles us. FatSher : Come on. Let's have supper. Come, Suhas. Usually , it does have a message to convey. It has a plot (a beginning, a crisis and a resolution). However, there are certain differences with respect to time, number of characters, setting etc., The skit is more of an informal nature. The number of characters is less. C Reading A Tribute The Indian film industry has completed a hundred years in the year 2013. It is a fitting tribute to the wAorld of cinema to recollect our favourite films, producers, N directors, actors, and music and art directors. A Telugu audiences are proud of many great prodGucers, directors and artistes. Savitri is one such prestigious artiste. Ever N since she was eight, she evinced interest in lAearning dance. Later she associated herself with the theatre. She formed a theatre L organization as well. She had little difficulty E in entering the film field. When Savitri was T twelve, she was offered a role in the film, Agnipareeksha, but was finally dropped as , she looked too young for the role. T She was given a song sequence- R Ranante rane ranu- in 'Pathala Bhairavi'. E Savitri's part in it was brief, but the effect of her performance was considerable. Her expressioCns were beautiful. A lot of film makers recognized 'a potential artiste' in her. SAs a result, she was elevated to the role of a heroine by the noted director L V Prasad in the film 'Samsaaram'(1950). On the sets, she was nervous; she had to repeat many takes and this proved a setback for her. The role was given to someone else and she was given a small role of less import. In the film 'Devadasu' (1953), [one of] the best picturisation[s] of Saratchandra Chatterjee's novel 'Devadas', Parvathi comes alive in Savitri. The young Parvathi with curly hair, a lock of hair straying to her forehead, the large round black berry eyes looking out from an innocent face left an indelible imprint in the minds of all cine lovers. She portrayed Devada's love and the role of a rich man's wife marvellously. Savitri left her mark in this evergreen Telugu classic. 126 Films and Theatre

Savitri established her credentials with 'Ardhangi'(1955) . She gave an exceptionally brilliant performance as a woman forced to marry a mentally retarded person (ANR). She nurses him back to health. She also teaches a lesson to her in-laws who conspire against her husband. A Savitri captured the audiences with N her charm and magnificent acting. She was A able to convey a wide range of feelings through her expressive eyes. Her G mischievous look - it captivates anyone; the look of fake anger provokes, the look filled with real anger pierces the heart. The look of passionN while waiting for her lover; the pain filled look when her love fails; the confident look that seems ready to face any situation, all A these myriad emotions are hidden in her eyes .The dimensions are endless and pages can be filled to describe the magic spell of her eyeLs. E Savitri's amazing talent was in full form in 'Missamma', a hit comedy that established Savitri's place firmly as a star. MTary in the film comes into an agreement with a Hindu youth, Nandamuri Taraka Ramarao (NTR) to pretend as a couple in order to get a job in a school. Mary was a Christian ,to the core, whereas Rao was a tolerant Hindu. What results in T is a three hour pure comedy for the audience! R Savitri was adored for the matchless ease in expression. Meena Kumari,the heroine of Hindi films Esaid, “when I watch Savitri's acting, I usually get doubts about my own acting". Her strikingly expressive eyes and her superb sense of timing made her one of the greatest C actresses. Amitabh Bacchan felt, 'Savitri was one of the first actresses with unbelievable spoSntaneity'. Maya Bazaar is another film that brought fame to Savitri. She played the role of Sasirekha. Recollecting the 16-annas Telugu lass clad in parikini, in the song 'allibilli ammayiki…' reminds us of the rich Telugu culture of yesteryears. In the final part of the film, Savitri plays the role of 127

maya (not real) Sasirekha (Ghatotkacha in disguise). She walks in a masculine manner imitating the legendary SV Ranga Rao acting as Ghatotkacha in the film to perfection. The theatre rocks with laughter when Lakshmana Kumara (Relangi) is teased by maya Sasirekha. She switches from the feminine to the mAasculine in the twinkling of an eye and needless to say, a female artiste N displaying masculine demon qualities with a club in hand has no parallel. A Savitri gets totaGlly involved in whatever role she plays. 'Chivaraku Migiledi' is one such film. She played N the role of a nurse in a psychiatry ward. In a particular scene the nAurse has a nervous breakdown and cries uncontrollably. The shot was over. "CUT", the director said, but Savitri who played the role L could not stop crying! Everyone in the set had to run to her and pacify her. The film became E a milestone in her career!! T Savitri was awarded the title 'Mahanati' (the Supreme artiste). She also received the Presidential award for her performance in 'Chivaraku Migiledi', the magnum opus of Savitri. , She was the recipient of T'Kalaimamani' and 'Nadigayar Tilakam' from Tamil film industry. Savitri had nearly 300 films to her credit. Her career was nearly 30 year long. She was R equally admired by Telugu and Tamil film lovers. She also acted in a few Kannada and Hindi E films. She had a lion's share of films when she was at the zenith of her career. Her passion for filmsC was so strong that she directed and produced a few films, in spite of certain adversities. S Savitri was a humane artiste. She was generous to the people who were in need. Once, she donated all the jewellery she was wearing to the Prime Minister's fund. Her rise as a star was like a meteor. She left the world in 1981 leaving an envied and unsurpassed legacy behind her. Savitri is no more. But she is among us with her unforgettable roles. Her versatility lives on and on and on. Paying tribute to her, the director and producer Dasari Narayana Rao said: 128 Films and Theatre

"... Many artistes are forgotten soon after the death. But, it is not so with Savitri. SHE WILL BE REMEMBERED AS LONG AS CELLULOID LIVES ON. 'All her films would amount to an 'Album of life' due to their range of themes; they encompass human lives and passions in their full diversity. What is cinema? Is it a fiction or a reality? Many people say many things. But Savitri gave a different definition. She said that cinema is ' Life'. Life is eternal. So is cinema because life runs through it. AND SAVITRI IS ETERNAL SINCE SHE GAVE THAT LIFE TO CINEMA." A N Glossary A magnum opus (n) : the greatest workG 16-annas Telugu lass (idiom): an expressiNon which means a perfect Telugu girl. lion's share (idiom) : majorA portion / part L zenith (n) : peak E Comprehension T , Answer the following questions. T 1. Have you everR seen any of the films in which Savitri acted? List them. Which of them do you like most? E 2. Savitri's qualities and her acting have been mentioned in the tribute. Which of Savitri's C qualities fascinates you most? S 3. Why was Savitri taken away from her main role in the film, 'Samsaaram'? 4. How do you think Savitri was able to strike back after she was replaced from the main role in 'Samsaaram'? 5. The purpose of the tribute is ...(choose the appropriate answer) a) to sympathize with Savitri b) to admire Savitri's acting and her abilities. c) to understand savitri's acting and qualities d) to express different opinions about Savitri 129

A Telugu audiences are proud of many great prodGucers, directors and artistes. Savitri is one such prestigious artiste. Ever N since she was eight, she evinced interest in lAearning dance. Later she associated herself with the theatre. She formed a theatre L organization as well. She had little difficulty E in entering the film field. When Savitri was T twelve, she was offered a role in the film, Agnipareeksha, but was finally dropped as , she looked too young for the role. T She was given a song sequence- R Ranante rane ranu- in 'Pathala Bhairavi'. E Savitri's part in it was brief, but the effect of her performance was considerable. Her expressioCns were beautiful. In the sentence above 'breathe one's last' is an idiomatic expression which means 'to die'. 150 Social Issues We have already learnt that an idiom is a mode of expression peculiar to a language. It is a group of words in a fixed order that has a particular meaning that is different from the meanings of each word understood on its own. Idioms cannot be translated word for word. They have become fixed through regular use with their figurative meanings. They should be used in their correct forms without dropping, adding or replacing any word. Study Skills Here are the words of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar on caste system. Read the text carefully and make notes on it. Suggest a suitable title. There are other special features of the caste system which have their evil effects and which militate against Democracy. One such special feature of the caste system lies in its A being accompanied by what is called "graded inequality". Castes are not equal in their status. They are standing one above another. They are jealous of one another.N It is an ascending and descending scale of contempt. This feature of the caste system has most pernicious A consequences. It destroys willing and helpful co-operation. G Caste and class differ in the fact that in the class there is no complete isolation as there is in the caste system. This is the second evil eNffect in the caste system accompanied by inequality. This manifests itself in the fact that the stimulus and response between two A castes is only one-sided. The higher caste act in one recognized way and the lower caste L must respond in established way. It means that when there is no equitable opportunity to receive the stimulus from and to returEn the response from different caste, the result is that the influence which educates some into masters, educates others into slaves. The experience T of each party loses its meaning when the free interchange of varying modes of life experience is arrested. It results into a separation of society, into a privileged and a subject class. Such , T a separation prevents endosmosis. R There is the third characteristic of the caste system which depicts the evils thereof which cuts at Ethe very roots of democracy. It is that one caste is bound to one occupation. Society is no doubt stably organized when each individual is doing that for which he has C aptitude by nature in such a way as to be useful to others; and that it is the business of S society to discover these aptitudes and progressively to train them for social use. But there is in a man an indefinite pluralities of capacities and activities which may characterize an individual. Stratification is stunting of the growth of the individual and deliberate stunting is deliberate denial of democracy. Or you can use reported speech: A Ram said that he was feeling ill. N It is not always necessary to change the verb in reported speech. If you report something and the situation hasn't changed, you need not chaAnge the verb to the past: Direct : Neelima said, 'My new job is Gvery interesting.' Reported : Neelima said that her neNw job is very interesting. (The situation hasn't changed. Her jobA is still interesting.) L Direct : Ravi said, 'I want to go to New York next year.' T (Ravi still wants to go to New York next year.) , T You can also change the verb to the past: R Neelima said that her new job was very interesting. E Ravi said that he wanted to go to New York the following year. C The past simple (did/saw/knew etc.) can usually remain the same in reported speech, S or you can change it into past perfect (had done/had seen/had known etc.): Direct : Ravi said: 'I woke up feeling ill, so I didn't go to work." Oral Discourse: Debate - “Human beings pose a great threat to the nature” - comment. 164 Bio-Diversity A Reading Environment (Interview with Wangari Maathai, Environmental Activist and Nobel Prize winner) Wangari Maathai started the Green Belt Movement and also fought for equal rights for women in Africa. She is the first African woman to win the NobAel Peace Prize. Read the excerpts from her interview N with Nippon Hoso Kyokai (NHK) Radio (Japan). A NHK Radio : How did you G become aware of the environment? N Wangari Maathai: From the time we started, we were trying to A respond to the basic needs of people L in the rural areas; and people were E asking for clean drinking water, for food, for energy (which is moTstly firewood), for building material, for , fodder for the animals. And all these come from the land. So we knew that what the people T in the rural areas were asking for had to do with the environment. They did not have those R things because the environment was degraded. So, from the very beginning we understood that we have to rehabilitate the environment. E The forested mountains were the source of water and the source of rain, so when C you deforest, you cause a shortage of water and a change of rainfall patterns and therefore peoSple are not able to get food and water. Therefore, in order for them to have good environment that can sustain their livelihoods, it is important to have a government that accounts to them, that protects them, that protects their interests, that is concerned about their lives. NHK Radio : How is peace connected to a good environment? W M : Many wars that are fought in the world are fought over natural resources. Some wars are fought because the environment is so degraded that it is not able to support communities and so they fight over the little that is left. Others are fought because some people want to take a lot of the resources, to control them, and to keep many other people out. 165 A N A G N Now whether this happens at the nationaAl level or at the regional level, or even at the global level, sooner or later there is discontent; and when that discontent is strong enough, L there is conflict. So good management of the natural resources, equitable distribution of E these resources, is important for peace. At the same time, good management of the natural resources is not possible if you dTo not have democratic space, respect for human beings, respect for human rights, giving other people dignity. , That is why the thTree themes are related, like the African stool, with three legs and the basin on which you sit. The three legs: one leg is peace, the other leg is good governance, R the third leg is sustainable management of resources. When you have those three legs, now E you can put the basin, which is development. And if you try to balance that stool without those three, it won't happen. C We have not shared our resources equitably. We have allowed some people, S especially those in power, to acquire a lot at the expense of the majority. And we have also engaged in conflict. NHK Radio : What was the environment like when you were young, and how did you go about saving it? W M. : When I was a child, which is almost more than fifty years ago, the environment was very pristine, very beautiful, and very green. We were a British colony, and the British government at that time started to clear cut the indigenous forests in our forested mountains because they wanted to establish commercial plantations of exotic species of trees such as 166 Bio-Diversity the pines from the northern hemisphere and the eucalyptus from Australia. These trees are very nice, they grow tall, and they grow very fast, but as they grow they destroy all the local biological diversity. All the flora and fauna disappeared. So although we were getting commercial timber for the growing timber industry, we also destroyed our A local flora and fauna. N As a result, these forests, which were the water towers, were no longer able to contain the A water, so when the rains fell the water ran G downstream and ended up in the lakes and oceans instead of going down into the underground N reservoir so that it could come back to us in the form of rivers. One thing we noted is that not onAly did the rain patterns change, became less, but also the rivers started drying up. We lost our L local biological diversity. So that's a lot of damage to our environment. E That is why in 1975, at the very first United Nations Conference for Women in T Mexico, many of the women were saying, "We need food, we need water, we need clean drinking water, we need fodde,r for our animals." And I was wondering, what has happened? T These are things that were there twenty years ago when I was a child. The environment had changed; and that'sR when I started this campaign to restore the vegetation and to restore the land and to rehabilitate the forests. E NHK Radio : What happened when you started working with the women? C W M.: Well, the first S time when I told them, "Let us plant trees", the women said they did not know how to plant trees. So I asked the foresters to come and teach them, but they were very complicated-they are professionals. It became very complicated for ordinary illiterate women so I told the women, "We shall use our 167 common sense, and just do what we do with other seeds." Women work on the farms. They're the ones who plant. They're the ones who cultivate. They're the ones who produce food, so I told them that seeds of trees are like any other A seeds. So if they were to treat these tree seeds the same way they treat N other seeds of food crops, there is A no difference. I told them to look foGr old broken pots even and put seeds there. They will germinate and they will know these are the seedlings from the seeds N they planted and we gave them plastic bags to be able to put those seedlings and to nurture them and when they were about half a meter long then they could go and transplant them on A their farms. L In the beginning it was difficult, but they soon gained confidence and they became E very competent foresters. So I called them "Foresters without Diplomas". T NHK Radio: Why do you think they responded so well to your message? , W M: It was a nTeed. When the women said they needed firewood and building material, we responded to that need. Plant trees; then you will have trees for firewood. In R the tropics, trees grow very fast. In five to ten years these trees serve as firewood, as E building materials. C Once we had planted those trees, we saw the need for them to understand why we havSe to have good governance; so it became important to give them civic education so that they could understand how we govern ourselves, why we govern ourselves the way we govern ourselves, why we are managing our environment the way we are managing it. Because we were dealing with the environment, we gave them education both in civics and also in environment. That made them understand clearly why they should take up the responsibility of protecting their environment-that it was not the responsibility of the government or the responsibility of somebody else to come and rehabilitate their environment on their own land. It's them; it's their responsibility. NHK Radio : What transformations did you see? 168 Bio-Diversity W M: One of the bigger transformations that I saw was that ability of an ordinary, illiterate woman to get to understand and to be able to plant trees that in five or ten years became big trees and she was able to cut them and be able to give herself energy; to be able to sell those trees and give herself an income; to be able to feel confident that she had done something for herself. That sense of pride, sense of dignity that they are not begging, that they are doing things for themselves was very empowering. That transformation was very powerful. A The other is the transformation of the landscape. Places where there was dust, there N are no more dust. There are trees, even birds and rabbits. They come back and they make the environment very beautiful. There is a shade and sometimAes even dry springs come back because the water is not running, the water is going into the ground. Very profound G transformation. N And the other transformation that I saw was the willingness of the people to fight for their rights; to decide that they have a right to a gAood clean environment; to decide that they will fight for their forests, they will protect their forests, and they will not allow corrupt L leaders to take their public land. E NHK Radio : How do you think you can influence the rest of Africa? T W M: Our efforts will in spire other people to stop wasting their resources and their , youth in wars and instead engage in creating a peaceful environment, more peaceful states. T I'm very hapRpy about the fact that now in Africa you see new efforts of ensuring that Africans engage in dialogue, that they invest in peaceful negotiations for conflicts, that we E manage our environment. We must restore our environment and try to ensure that we do not fight,C because we are allowing the environment, especially the land, to be degraded; and then we fight over agricultural land and grazing land. I see a lot of hope in what is happening S in Somalia, what is happening in the Sudan, what is happening in West Africa. I see a lot of African leaders encouraging each other to engage in dialogue. NHK Radio : What is the one thing we can do ? W M : For me, my greatest activity is to plant a tree. I think that a tree is a wonderful symbol for the environment and when we plant a tree we plant hope. We plant the future for ourselves, for our children, for the birds. We plant something that will last, long after we are gone. Reported speech Apart from the ground rules that are laid down for reporting in traditional grammar books, there are certain other principles that are to be followed to make the speech appealing. 176 Bio-Diversity Suppose you want to tell somebody what Ram said. There are two ways of doing this: You can repeat Ram's words (direct speech). Ram said, 'I am feeling ill.' Or you can use reported speech: A Ram said that he was feeling ill. N It is not always necessary to change the verb in reported speech. If you report something and the situation hasn't changed, you need not chaAnge the verb to the past: Direct : Neelima said, 'My new job is Gvery interesting.' Reported : Neelima said that her neNw job is very interesting. (The situation hasn't changed. Her jobA is still interesting.) L Direct : Ravi said, 'I want to go to New York next year.' T (Ravi still wants to go to New York next year.) , T You can also change the verb to the past: R Neelima said that her new job was very interesting. Effects of soil pollution are dangerous. They may E cause acid rains which can kill trees and other plants. C It disrupts the balance of nature. Soil pollution is also dangerous to wild life. pages.text: C Reading A Tale of Three Villages 1. Koko Village, Nigeria A Mr. Sunday Nana, his wife and four smNall children live in Koko Village, Nigeria . The A village is like any other African vGillage-picturesque, colourful and noisy. The Nana family's house N too, is the same as all the other Ahouses in the village, with mud walls and a rusting corrugated iron L roof, and with children and E chickens sharing the compound. T There is one difference, however. Outside Mr. Nana's front are three large empty metal drums, the bright red paint , now flaking away, but thTe skull and crossbones symbol clearly visible on each. And in a clearing 200m away from the village, next to a stream that the villagers get their drinking R water from, is an enormous pyramid of identical drums, reaching to the sky. Some of them E are badly corroded, their slimy contents of various colours - grey, dark green, bright orange, etc. - leaking out, down, on to the baked African earth and into the stream. Some have fallen C down and rolled - or been rolled by playful children - into the bush. Some are smoking in S the midday heat. Some are swelling, as if their contents are bursting to get out. Some have already burst. “They came on a Wednesday,” said Sunday, “Many, many big lorries. They took all day unloading them. No-one told us what was in them. They gave the Chief a brown paper bag-I saw him smiling as the lorries drove away. This was five years ago. Then three months ago, one of the brightest boys in the village - Thomas Agonyo - started university in Lagos. He came home one weekend with a new Chemistry book, and spent all day looking at the drums and writing things down and talking to himself and shaking his head. We all thought he had gone mad. Then he called a meeting of the village and told us that the drums contained 186 Bio-Diversity

poisonous chemicals. He said they had come from Italy. But I don't know where that is. Is it in Europe?” Mr. Sunday Nana stopped, frowning, a troubled look on his face, "In the last five years, 13 people have died in this village, my own elder brother one of them. They have been in pain, terrible pain. We have never seen deaths like that before. Lots of our children are sick. We have asked the Government to take the drums away, but they do nothing. We have written to Italy, but they do nothing. The Chief says we should movAe our houses to another place. But we have no money to buy land. We have no choice. We have to stay N here. “And they” ------ pointing to the mountain of death in the clearing - "are our neighbours." A Comprehension G N I. Answer the following questions. A 1. Why were the large empty drums placed outside Mr. Nana's house? L 2. What harm can the pyramid of identical drums cause to the villagers? E 3. Why was the Chief smiling as the lorries drove away? T 4. Was Thomas Agonyo correct in his findings? Justify your opinion. 5. Why didn't the people mo,ve from their place? T 6. There is a repetition of sentences with 'some' in the passage. Read the passage again and R write down the sentences and the function of 'some' in each one of them. Do you find E any other repetitions in the passage? If yes, mention it. C S II. Choose the correct answer. 1. A Grammar N Quantifiers as the name implies are a type of determiners which denote imprecise A quantity. They differ from numbers or numerals which indicate precise quantity. G Example: I've got some apples in my basket and some water inN my bottle. I haven't got any apples in my basket, nor any water in my bottle. A Generally quantifiers are used before nouns. L Some, any, all, no, no one, both, each, every, several are some of the quantifiers. E "Some" is usually thought of as the positive counterpart to "any" in many circumstances. T "Any" can be used before countable and uncountable nouns usually in questions and negative sentences. , T Example: R 1. Are you bringing any friends with you? E 2. I am bringing some friends with me. C Quantifiers come before nouns. Some of the quantifiers you find in the text are: some, any, no. You also find numerals. Pick out the nouns along with quantifiers and numerals S and write them down and analyze the meaning they convey. 2. ___________meteorologists predict that the world will get warm between 2 to 4 degrees Celsius by the year 2030. The scientists believe that ___________year___________ polar ice will melt and cause rainfall, increase in the sea level and also temperature will be affected.___________people disagree with the theory that the human activity is having an effect on the world's climate.___________scientists need to monitor the Earth's atmosphere and ___________human beings need to care for the air, water and plant life that influence A world's weather. So for___________argument G there is a counter argument. ___________ individual differs with the other in ___________ way or the other. N 2. Ponnimanthuri Village, India A "I can remember the time," she L said wistfully, "when all the fieldsE around this village were green and the T harvests good". Her outstretched arm described a complete circle as she , stood in the morning sunT. "Then they built those monsters, those……." Her R voice spluttered in anger as she shook E her fist at a collection of ominous- looking black buildings on the horizon, C covered in a low-lying shroud of thick S smoke. "They said that factories need leather to make shoes, handbags and clothes. They said our menfolk would get jobs. They said we would all become rich." We stood silent, each thinking our own thoughts. Yes, they told you all that. But there is so much they didn't tell you. They didn't tell you that to change animal skins into leather - which they call tanning - uses as many as 250 different chemicals, including heavy metals such as cadmium , arsenic and chromium. They didn't tell you that these chemicals are discharged into the environment from those chimney stacks and fall to earth for miles around, polluting the earth below. They didn't tell you that this would poison your fields, so that nothing will grow. 189

“They didn't tell us that the chemicals would be dumped in open fields and into our rivers,” sighed Vijayasama. We had been thinking the same thoughts. “They didn't tell us that our women would have to walk ten kilometres every day. They didn't tell us that we would get ulcer and sores on A our bodies. They didn't tell us…” Her voice trailed off. There is so much they didn't N tell you, I thought. A “We don't buy leather shoes or leather handbags or leather clothes,” she said. G N Glossary A outstretched (v) : pulled out to full length L trailed off (phr. verb) : became gradually quieter and then stopped E T I. Answer the following questions. 1. The people in this village w,ere affected by chemical factories. Where should the factories T be built according to you? Why? R 2. The nCarrator said at the end, "There is so much they didn't tell you, I thought"-what was that so much that was not told, according to you? S Grammar Write the following sentences in reported speech. 1. "I can remember the time." she said wistfully, "when all the fields around this village were green and the harvests good." 2. "They said that factories need leather to make shoes, handbags and clothes. They said our men folk would get jobs. They said we would all become rich." 190 Bio-Diversity

3. Vorobyov Village, Ukraine (formerly USSR) "It happened on April the 26th 1986. I remember the date because it was my mother's birthday. We heard the explosion early in the morning. We didn't worry, because there had been explosions before from Chernobyl. But this one was bigger. Everyone stopped what they were doing and listened. Then we ran out into A the garden. We could see a cloud of white smoke coming from the nuclear reactor." NatashaN Revenko wiped her hands nervously on her apron. Tears came to the corners A of her eyes, and slid slowly down her pinched, pale cheeks. "It was a Saturday," she went on, still wiping her handGs on her apron. "It was a lovely warm day, and the children N played outside all weekend. Even when the dust began to fall, they still played outside. They picked up handfuls of it A and threw it at each other, laughing. It was Wednesday before L the loudspeaker van came to the village, telling us to keep our children indoors and not to touch tEhe radioactive dust. They also told us to wash down our houses and roads with water. A week later the children began to vomit. Their hair fell T out. They couldn't eat. They grew so thin, and sores appeared all over their little bodies. Two weeks after that, all three died - all three on the same day." She broke down now and , cried quietly, as she hadT done so many times before. "They're buried over there." She pointed to the church graveyard. "Lots of village children are. And adults." R I touched her gently on the shoulder, leaving her to her bitter-sweet memories, and E walked on through the silence. It was a ghost town. No one lived there anymore. They had either diCed or been forcibly evacuated. The fields were barren. Nothing grew. Nothing ever would again. There was no bird-song. No rabbit peered at me. No cow endlessly S chewed. No horse neighed. Natasha caught me up as we boarded the bus marked MOSCOW. "Thank you for coming with me," She said. "I wanted to see the graves and the house again, before I die." A Reading Read the following extract from Wings of Fire, where the former President of India speaks of his childhood. My Childhood A I was born into a middle - class Tamil family in the island town of Rameswaram in the erstwhile Madras State. My father, Jainulabdeen , had neither mNuch formal education nor much wealth; despite these disadvantages, he possessed great innate wisdom and a true A generosity of spirit. He had an ideal helpmate in my mother, Ashiamma. I do not recall the G exact number of people she fed every day, but I am quite certain that far more outsiders ate with us than all the members of our own family put together. N I was one of the children - a short boy with rather undistinguished looks, born to tall A and handsome parents. We lived in our ancestral house, which was built in the middle of the L nineteenth century. It was a fairly large pucca house , made of limestone and brick, on the Mosque Street in Rameswaram. My aEustere father used to avoid all inessential comforts and luxuries. However , all necessities were provided for, in terms of food, medicine or T clothes. In fact, I would say mine was a very secure childhood, both materially and emotionally. , T R E C S 197

The Second World War broke out in 1939, when I was eight years old. For reasons I have never been able to understand, a sudden demand for tamarind seeds erupted in the market. I used to collect the seeds and sell them to a provision shop on Mosque Street. A day's collection would fetch me the princely sum of one anna. My brother -in-law Jallaluddin would tell me stories about the War which I would later attempt to trace in the headlines in Dinamani. Our area, being isolated, was completely unaffected by the War. But soon India was forced to join the Allied Forces and something like a state of emergency was declared. The first casualty came in the form of the suspension of the train halt at RameAswaram station. The newspapers now had to be bundled and thrown out from the moving train on the N Rameswaram Road between Rameswaram and Dhanuskodi. That forced my cousin Samsuddin, who distributed newspapers in Rameswaram, to look for a helpinAg hand to catch the bundles and, as if naturally, I filled the slot. Samsuddin helped me earn my first wages. Half a century G later, I can still feel the surge of pride in earning my own money for the first time. N Every child is born, with some inherited characteristics, into a specific socio- economic and emotional environment, and trainAed in certain ways by figures of authority. I inherited honesty and self-discipline from my father; from my mother, I inherited faith in L goodness and deep kindness and so did my three brothers and sister. I had three close friends E in my childhood - Ramanadha Sastry, Aravindan and Sivaprakasan. All these boys were from T , T R E C S 198 Nation and Diversity

orthodox Hindu Brahmin families. As children, none of us ever felt any difference amongst ourselves because of our religious differences and upbringing. In fact, Ramanadha Sastry was the son of Pakshi Lakshmana Sastry, the high priest of the Rameswaram temple. Later he took over the priesthood of the Rameswaram temple from his father; Aravindan went into the business of arranging transport for visiting pilgrims; and Sivaprakasan became a catering contractor for the Southern Railways. During the annual Shri Sita Rama Kalyanam ceremony, our familyA used to arrange boats with a special platform for carrying idols of the Lord from the temple to the marriage N site, situated in the middle of the pond called Rama Tirtha which was near our house. Events from the Ramayana and from the life of the Prophet were the bAedtime stories my mother and grandmother would tell the children in our family. G One day when I was in the fifth standard at the Rameswaram Elementary School, a N new teacher came to our class. I used to wear a cap which marked me as a Muslim, and I always sat in the front row next to Ramanadha sAastry, who wore the sacred thread. The new teacher could not stomach a Hindu priest's son sitting with a Muslim boy. In accordance L with our social ranking as the new teacher saw it, I was asked to go and sit on the back bench. E I felt very sad, and so did Ramanadha Sastry. He looked utterly downcast as I shifted to my seat in the last row. The image ofT him weeping when I shifted to the last row left a lasting impression on me. , After school, weT went home and told our respective parents about the incident. Lakshmana Sastry summoned the teacher, and in our presence, told the teacher that he should R not spread the poison of social inequality and communal intolerance in the minds of innocent E children. He bluntly asked the teacher to either apologize or quit the school and the island. Not only did the teacher regret his behaviour but the strong sense of conviction Lakshmana C Sastry conveyed ultimately reformed this young teacher. S On the whole, the small society of Rameswaram was very rigid in terms of the segregation of different social groups. However, my science teacher Sivasubramania Iyer, though an orthodox Brahmin with a very conservative wife, was something of a rebel. He did his best to break social barriers so that people from varying backgrounds could mingle easily. He used hours with me and would say, "Kalam, I want you to develop so that you are on par with the highly educated people of the big cities." One day, he invited me to his home for a meal. His wife was horrified at the idea of a Muslim boy being invited to dine in her ritually pure kitchen. She refused to serve me in her kitchen. Sivasubramania Iyer was not perturbed, nor did he get angry with his wife, but 199

A N A G N A L instead, served me with his own hands and sat down beside me to eat his meal. His wife watched us from behind the kitchenE door. I wondered whether she had observed any difference in the way I ate rice, drank water or cleaned the floor after the meal. When I was T leaving his house, Sivasubramania Iyer invited me to join him for dinner again the next weekend. Observing my hesitation, he told not to get upset, saying, “Once you decide to , change the system, such pTroblems have to be confronted.” When I visited his house the next week, SivasubramaRnia Iyer’s wife took me inside her kitchen and served me food with her own hands. C Reading Unity in Diversity in India India, a country of many ethnic groups, is a land of myriad languages, a veritable babel of tongues and numerous modes of apparel. For the most part, the continental A dimensions of the country account for these variations and diversities. Besides, there are several religions, sects and beliefs. But there are certain common linNks and uniting bonds that people have sought to develop in order to achieve the eminently desirable goal of unity A amidst diversity. G It is true that superficial observers are likely to be bewildered by the astonishing variety of Indian life. They fail to discover the one inN many, the individual in the aggregate; the simple in the composite. With them the whole is lost in its parts. What is needed is the A superior interpretation, synthesis of the power of the mind that can give rise to a vision of the whole. L E T , T R E C S A keen penetrating insight will not fail to recognise the fundamental unity beneath the manifold variety in India. The diversity itself, far from being a damaging cause of disunity and weakness, is a fertile source of strength and wealth. Sir Herbert Risely has rightly observed: "Beneath the manifold diversity of physical and social types, languages, customs and religions which strike the observer in India, there can still be discerned a certain underlying uniformity of life from the Himalayas to Cape Comorin." From his long and first-hand experience in India, Vincent A. Smith says that the civilisation of India has many features which differentiate it from that of the other regions 214 Nation and Diversity

A N A G N A L E of the world, while they are common to the whole country in degree sufficient to justify its treatment as a unity in the historyT of human, social and intellectual development. Even the early Indian his tory unmistakably shows that the political consciousness of , the people has from the vTery early times, grasped the whole of India as a unit and assimilated the entire area as the theatre of its activities. India is not a mere geographical expression, R nor is it a mere collection of separate people, traditions and conventions. India is much more than thisE. The best proof lies in the fact that Indian history has quickened into life. InCdia has many races, castes, sub-castes, nationalities and communities, but the heart of India is one. We are all heirs to a common and rich culture. Our cultural heritage consists S of our art and literature as they flourished centuries ago. Our cultural heritage serves as a bond of unity between people of different faiths and creeds. The streams of different cultures have flowed into our subcontinent to make us what we are and what we will be. There were Dravidians in India before the coming of the Aryans and Hinduism is a blend of the cultures of the North and the South. India has one hundred and fifty dialects, and twenty-two recognised regional languages, but Hindi, like English, has come to stay as the lingua franca of our nation. From Kashmir to Kanyakumari and from Mumbai to Nagaland, Hindi is now understood and is recognised as the national language of India. 215

India has a rich cultural heritage. We are inheritors of several grand treasures in the fields of music, fine arts, dance, drama, theatre and sculpture. Our sages and seers have left behind a tradition of A piety, penance, spiritual greatness, conquest of N passion, etc. Our scriptures are A the storehouses of spiritual Gwisdom. Our saints aspired to the realisation of the infinite. We have inherited great spiritual values contrasted with which N the materialistic progress of the West appears insignificant. The West has to learn a lot from India, anAd it has now been realised when people in the United States and Europe are turning to the Indian way of life. Indian yogis and maharishis, L musicians and spiritual leaders E have all attracted them in a big way. A significant move to projectT India's cultural unity has been the , holding of Festivals of India in T various parts of the world. The R West is fast inclining towards our spiritual values which include E meditation and contemplation, C charity and love, universal brotSherhood and fear of God, piety and unselfishness, control of passions and peace of mind. Our cultural unity is further exemplified by the temples of the South and of Khajuraho, the caves of Ajanta and Ellora, which are shining examples of India's proficiency in sculpture and architecture. Our music has come to enjoy worldwide popularity. Indian classical music, like the Indian dances, is built on the concept of ragas and talas. Each raga is regarded appropriate to a certain time of the day or the night. There are believed to be about 250 ragas in common use in the North as well as in the South. In the modern 216 Nation and Diversity

times, people like Ravi Shankar have taken Indian music to the West and thus bridged the gap between the music of the East and the West. Other significant features of India's cultural unity A are the variety, colour and the N emotional richness of its dances. The country abounds in tribal dances, old-dances as well as classical dances of A great virtuosity. Throughout India, dance is regarded not merely as an accompaniment to G social intercourse, but also as a mode of aesthetic expression and spiritual realization. The great symbol of dance is Shiva, the CosmNic Dancer, depicted in sculpture and poetry as Nataraja. Similarly, the classical theatre in India has a history of more than two A thousand years. It was performed in palaces and in temples. The classical plays combined L music and dance. Tragedy was, and is, still discouraged otherwise; the range of themes covered is wide. E It is this strand of cultural uTnity running through the country that we are heir to, and to which people in the West are increasingly turning now. It is up to the younger generation to uphold this torch of cultur,al unity for the rest of the world to see, follow and emulate, T and not get dazed by the superficial prosperity and material achievement of the West, where R man has set foot on the Moon in his quest for space travel, but finds himself isolated in his own society and community. Some of them E are badly corroded, their slimy contents of various colours - grey, dark green, bright orange, etc. - leaking out, down, on to the baked African earth and into the stream. Some have fallen C down and rolled - or been rolled by playful children - into the bush. Some are smoking in S the midday heat. Some are swelling, as if their contents are bursting to get out. Each raga is regarded appropriate to a certain time of the day or the night. There are believed to be about 250 ragas in common use in the North as well as in the South. In the modern 216 Nation and Diversity times, people like Ravi Shankar have taken Indian music to the West and thus bridged the gap between the music of the East and the West. Other significant features of India's cultural unity A are the variety, colour and the N emotional richness of its dances. The country abounds in tribal dances, old-dances as well as classical dances of A great virtuosity. Throughout India, dance is regarded not merely as an accompaniment to G social intercourse, but also as a mode of aesthetic expression and spiritual realization. The great symbol of dance is Shiva, the CosmNic Dancer, depicted in sculpture and poetry as Nataraja. Similarly, the classical theatre in India has a history of more than two A thousand years. It was performed in palaces and in temples. The classical plays combined L music and dance. Tragedy was, and is, still discouraged otherwise; the range of themes covered is wide. E It is this strand of cultural uTnity running through the country that we are heir to, and to which people in the West are increasingly turning now. It is up to the younger generation to uphold this torch of cultur,al unity for the rest of the world to see, follow and emulate, T and not get dazed by the superficial prosperity and material achievement of the West, where R man has set foot on the Moon in his quest for space travel, but finds himself isolated in his own society and community. My Childhood A I was born into a middle - class Tamil family in the island town of Rameswaram in the erstwhile Madras State. My father, Jainulabdeen , had neither mNuch formal education nor much wealth; despite these disadvantages, he possessed great innate wisdom and a true A generosity of spirit. He had an ideal helpmate in my mother, Ashiamma. I do not recall the G exact number of people she fed every day, but I am quite certain that far more outsiders ate with us than all the members of our own family put together. N I was one of the children - a short boy with rather undistinguished looks, born to tall A and handsome parents. We lived in our ancestral house, which was built in the middle of the L nineteenth century. It was a fairly large pucca house , made of limestone and brick, on the Mosque Street in Rameswaram. My aEustere father used to avoid all inessential comforts and luxuries. However , all necessities were provided for, in terms of food, medicine or T clothes. In fact, I would say mine was a very secure childhood, both materially and emotionally. , T R E C S 197 The Second World War broke out in 1939, when I was eight years old. For reasons I have never been able to understand, a sudden demand for tamarind seeds erupted in the market. I used to collect the seeds and sell them to a provision shop on Mosque Street. A day's collection would fetch me the princely sum of one anna. My brother -in-law Jallaluddin would tell me stories about the War which I would later attempt to trace in the headlines in Dinamani. Our area, being isolated, was completely unaffected by the War. But soon India was forced to join the Allied Forces and something like a state of emergency was declared. The first casualty came in the form of the suspension of the train halt at RameAswaram station. The newspapers now had to be bundled and thrown out from the moving train on the N Rameswaram Road between Rameswaram and Dhanuskodi. That forced my cousin Samsuddin, who distributed newspapers in Rameswaram, to look for a helpinAg hand to catch the bundles and, as if naturally, I filled the slot. Samsuddin helped me earn my first wages. Half a century G later, I can still feel the surge of pride in earning my own money for the first time. N Every child is born, with some inherited characteristics, into a specific socio- economic and emotional environment, and trainAed in certain ways by figures of authority. I inherited honesty and self-discipline from my father; from my mother, I inherited faith in L goodness and deep kindness and so did my three brothers and sister. I had three close friends E in my childhood - Ramanadha Sastry, Aravindan and Sivaprakasan. All these boys were from T , T R E C S 198 Nation and Diversity orthodox Hindu Brahmin families. As children, none of us ever felt any difference amongst ourselves because of our religious differences and upbringing. In fact, Ramanadha Sastry was the son of Pakshi Lakshmana Sastry, the high priest of the Rameswaram temple. Later he took over the priesthood of the Rameswaram temple from his father; Aravindan went into the business of arranging transport for visiting pilgrims; and Sivaprakasan became a catering contractor for the Southern Railways. During the annual Shri Sita Rama Kalyanam ceremony, our familyA used to arrange boats with a special platform for carrying idols of the Lord from the temple to the marriage N site, situated in the middle of the pond called Rama Tirtha which was near our house. Events from the Ramayana and from the life of the Prophet were the bAedtime stories my mother and grandmother would tell the children in our family. G One day when I was in the fifth standard at the Rameswaram Elementary School, a N new teacher came to our class. I used to wear a cap which marked me as a Muslim, and I always sat in the front row next to Ramanadha sAastry, who wore the sacred thread. The new teacher could not stomach a Hindu priest's son sitting with a Muslim boy. In accordance L with our social ranking as the new teacher saw it, I was asked to go and sit on the back bench. E I felt very sad, and so did Ramanadha Sastry. He looked utterly downcast as I shifted to my seat in the last row. The image ofT him weeping when I shifted to the last row left a lasting impression on me. , After school, weT went home and told our respective parents about the incident. Lakshmana Sastry summoned the teacher, and in our presence, told the teacher that he should R not spread the poison of social inequality and communal intolerance in the minds of innocent E children. He bluntly asked the teacher to either apologize or quit the school and the island. Not only did the teacher regret his behaviour but the strong sense of conviction Lakshmana C Sastry conveyed ultimately reformed this young teacher. S On the whole, the small society of Rameswaram was very rigid in terms of the segregation of different social groups. However, my science teacher Sivasubramania Iyer, though an orthodox Brahmin with a very conservative wife, was something of a rebel. He did his best to break social barriers so that people from varying backgrounds could mingle easily. He used hours with me and would say, "Kalam, I want you to develop so that you are on par with the highly educated people of the big cities." One day, he invited me to his home for a meal. His wife was horrified at the idea of a Muslim boy being invited to dine in her ritually pure kitchen. She refused to serve me in her kitchen. Sivasubramania Iyer was not perturbed, nor did he get angry with his wife, but 199

lessonSections.fullText: C Reading Unity in Diversity in India India, a country of many ethnic groups, is a land of myriad languages, a veritable babel of tongues and numerous modes of apparel. For the most part, the continental A dimensions of the country account for these variations and diversities. Besides, there are several religions, sects and beliefs. But there are certain common linNks and uniting bonds that people have sought to develop in order to achieve the eminently desirable goal of unity A amidst diversity. G It is true that superficial observers are likely to be bewildered by the astonishing variety of Indian life. They fail to discover the one inN many, the individual in the aggregate; the simple in the composite. With them the whole is lost in its parts. What is needed is the A superior interpretation, synthesis of the power of the mind that can give rise to a vision of the whole. L E T , T R E C S A keen penetrating insight will not fail to recognise the fundamental unity beneath the manifold variety in India. The diversity itself, far from being a damaging cause of disunity and weakness, is a fertile source of strength and wealth. Sir Herbert Risely has rightly observed: "Beneath the manifold diversity of physical and social types, languages, customs and religions which strike the observer in India, there can still be discerned a certain underlying uniformity of life from the Himalayas to Cape Comorin." From his long and first-hand experience in India, Vincent A. Smith says that the civilisation of India has many features which differentiate it from that of the other regions 214 Nation and Diversity A N A G N A L E of the world, while they are common to the whole country in degree sufficient to justify its treatment as a unity in the historyT of human, social and intellectual development. Even the early Indian his tory unmistakably shows that the political consciousness of , the people has from the vTery early times, grasped the whole of India as a unit and assimilated the entire area as the theatre of its activities. India is not a mere geographical expression, R nor is it a mere collection of separate people, traditions and conventions. India is much more than thisE. The best proof lies in the fact that Indian history has quickened into life. InCdia has many races, castes, sub-castes, nationalities and communities, but the heart of India is one. We are all heirs to a common and rich culture. Our cultural heritage consists S of our art and literature as they flourished centuries ago. Our cultural heritage serves as a bond of unity between people of different faiths and creeds. The streams of different cultures have flowed into our subcontinent to make us what we are and what we will be. There were Dravidians in India before the coming of the Aryans and Hinduism is a blend of the cultures of the North and the South. India has one hundred and fifty dialects, and twenty-two recognised regional languages, but Hindi, like English, has come to stay as the lingua franca of our nation. From Kashmir to Kanyakumari and from Mumbai to Nagaland, Hindi is now understood and is recognised as the national language of India. 215 India has a rich cultural heritage. We are inheritors of several grand treasures in the fields of music, fine arts, dance, drama, theatre and sculpture. Our sages and seers have left behind a tradition of A piety, penance, spiritual greatness, conquest of N passion, etc. Our scriptures are A the storehouses of spiritual Gwisdom. Our saints aspired to the realisation of the infinite. We have inherited great spiritual values contrasted with which N the materialistic progress of the West appears insignificant. The West has to learn a lot from India, anAd it has now been realised when people in the United States and Europe are turning to the Indian way of life. Indian yogis and maharishis, L musicians and spiritual leaders E have all attracted them in a big way. A significant move to projectT India's cultural unity has been the , holding of Festivals of India in T various parts of the world. The R West is fast inclining towards our spiritual values which include E meditation and contemplation, C charity and love, universal brotSherhood and fear of God, piety and unselfishness, control of passions and peace of mind. Our cultural unity is further exemplified by the temples of the South and of Khajuraho, the caves of Ajanta and Ellora, which are shining examples of India's proficiency in sculpture and architecture. Our music has come to enjoy worldwide popularity. Indian classical music, like the Indian dances, is built on the concept of ragas and talas. Each raga is regarded appropriate to a certain time of the day or the night. There are believed to be about 250 ragas in common use in the North as well as in the South. In the modern 216 Nation and Diversity times, people like Ravi Shankar have taken Indian music to the West and thus bridged the gap between the music of the East and the West. Other significant features of India's cultural unity A are the variety, colour and the N emotional richness of its dances. The country abounds in tribal dances, old-dances as well as classical dances of A great virtuosity. Throughout India, dance is regarded not merely as an accompaniment to G social intercourse, but also as a mode of aesthetic expression and spiritual realization. The great symbol of dance is Shiva, the CosmNic Dancer, depicted in sculpture and poetry as Nataraja. Similarly, the classical theatre in India has a history of more than two A thousand years. It was performed in palaces and in temples. The classical plays combined L music and dance. Tragedy was, and is, still discouraged otherwise; the range of themes covered is wide. E It is this strand of cultural uTnity running through the country that we are heir to, and to which people in the West are increasingly turning now. It is up to the younger generation to uphold this torch of cultur,al unity for the rest of the world to see, follow and emulate, T and not get dazed by the superficial prosperity and material achievement of the West, where R man has set foot on the Moon in his quest for space travel, but finds himself isolated in his own society and community. E C Glossary S ethnic (adj) : connected with / belonging to a nation, race or people that shares a cultural tradition myriad (adj) : an extremely large number of babel (n) : the sound of many voices talking at a time penetrate (v) : go into / through discern (v) : to know / recognize or understand 217
